1832–1920 · Germany

Wilhelm Wundt

German physician and philosopher. He organised one of the first psychology laboratories in Leipzig and trained a generation of researchers from around the world.

Biography

Wilhelm Wundt was born in 1832 in Neckarau, near Mannheim. He studied medicine and worked in Heidelberg as an assistant to Hermann von Helmholtz, where he became interested in the physiology of the senses. In 1873–1874 he published the Principles of Physiological Psychology, an attempt to gather what physiology could say about experience. In 1875 he took a chair in philosophy at Leipzig, and from 1879 he devoted a university room to psychological research with students, which the university formally recognised as an institute a few years later.

For more than forty years in Leipzig he supervised a huge number of doctoral theses, wrote tens of thousands of pages and received students from Europe, the United States and Asia. He died in 1920 in Grossbothen.

Questions he investigated

  • What elements is conscious experience made of, and how do they combine?
  • How long do mental processes take, and what makes them longer?
  • How do language, myths and customs, which cannot be studied in a laboratory, take shape?

Contributions

Wundt gave psychology an institution: a laboratory, a journal and a way of training people. He distinguished two complementary routes: the experimental one, for elementary processes, and the historical-cultural one (Völkerpsychologie), for higher processes. He developed the notion of apperception, the active process by which attention organises the contents of consciousness.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

His students included James McKeen Cattell, Edward Titchener, Emil Kraepelin, Oswald Külpe and Hugo Münsterberg. Several later moved away from his ideas: Külpe and the Würzburg school argued for imageless thought; Titchener built a narrower structuralism than his teacher's.

A documented anecdote

The famous photograph of Wundt with his group, seated beside a timing apparatus, became the official portrait of "scientific psychology". It is genuine, but it is staged: it shows how the new discipline wanted to present itself rather than an everyday scene in the laboratory.

Criticism, limits and reception

His image in English-language textbooks was partly built through Titchener, who presented him as an introspectionist focused on the elements of consciousness. Since the 1970s, historians such as Kurt Danziger and Arthur Blumenthal have shown a broader body of work, with a strong interest in will, culture and language.
